newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS - Stronger growth seen for Finland.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Stronger growth seen for Finland.

text.p: A stream of upbeat forecasts on Tuesday suggested Finland's already bright growth prospects have turned yet more bullish, and analysts remained confident growth would be solid despite a warning of possible overheating.
Merita, Finland's biggest bank, upgraded its 1997 growth forecast to four percent from 3.5 percent. A top finance ministry economist said five percent growth was within reach.
Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said the economic outlook was now better than at any time so far in the 1990s. The service industry said sales and profitability would increase in 1997. @

"We are clearly for the first time in a situation where growth expectations and confidence in a stable growth trend are in place simultaneously. A solid foundation like that has been sorely missed," Niinisto wrote in a newspaper column.

The Finnish markka took a breather after recent sharp gains -- partly thanks to central bank intervention, forex dealers said -- but Salomon Brothers said it was clearly undervalued and could firm to 2.95-2.90 German marks this year.
Government and other sources also sounded hopeful about prospects of reducing joblessness, Finland's thorniest problem and one of Europe's highest rates at 16.3 percent in 1996. @

"I see a great opportunity to reduce unemployment," Niinisto added. He made no reference to the government's target of halving joblessness to eight-nine percent by 1999, but a government committee said it still believed this could be done.
The top-level report by Finnish civil servants said annual economic growth projected around four percent would help Finland cut joblessness to about 12 percent by 1999.
On a more cautious note, it warned of the risk of overheating in the construction sector. @

"A too-rapid pace of growth in construction could lead to an uncontrolled rise in construction costs," it said, adding that due to this threat, construction investment should not be boosted by any economic policy means.
The Bank of Finland said last Friday that construction activity had picked up sharply in the latter part of 1996.

But Merita Bank chief economist Juha Ahtola remained sanguine. Presenting the bank's more upbeat forecasts for 1997, he said speedier Finnish growth did not look likely to put the economy out of balance. @
"Strength and stability are words that describe the Finnish economy now and in the period to come," Ahtola said.
And Salomon Brothers vice president and economist Wike Groenenberg, in Helsinki on a visit, said the overall risk of the economy overheating looked quite limited.
"With growth around four percent it could create problems in some areas, but is it enough to create overall price pressure? I'm not convinced," she told Reuters. @

Against this background, economists said Finland's central bank looks unlikely to use the interest rate tool to curb the markka's appreciation against the mark, at least until the markka climbs to 2.95 against the mark.
Instead, they said the central bank is in the short term likely to be quite comfortable intervening on the forex market to sell markka and add to its foreign currency reserves.
"If the markka strengthens to 2.95 per mark a rate cut would be back on the agenda," Merita Bank chief analyst Jukka Lepomaki said.
